questions.q: What mainly separates the three ways of asking a yes/no question in French?
questions.why: Intonation, est-ce que and inversion mean the same thing. Choosing between them is a social decision: spoken, neutral, formal.

questions.q: Turn « Tu aimes la musique. » into a question with est-ce que.
a: Est-ce que tu aimes la musique ?
Est-ce que tu aimes la musique?
Est-ce que tu aimes la musique
questions.why: Est-ce que bolts onto the front and changes nothing else, which is why it is the safest choice while learning. Que elides before a vowel: est-ce qu'il vient demain ?
Inversion swaps the verb and the subject pronoun and joins them with a hyphen: parlez-vous, viens-tu, sont-ils.
The -t- appears only when the verb ends in a vowel and the pronoun starts with one: va-t-il, arrive-t-elle. A final d or t already supplies it: dit-il, prend-il.
You never invert with je. Use est-ce que or intonation; the only survivors are fixed forms like puis-je, suis-je, ai-je, dois-je.

questions.q: Build the careful-style question: Where is Paul going?
questions.why: A noun subject cannot be inverted. It stays in place and a matching pronoun is added after the verb: Où Paul va-t-il ? Marie est-elle irlandaise ?
Moving the question word to the end makes it casual: tu vas où, tu pars quand, ça coûte combien. Extremely common in speech, wrong in writing.
Que becomes quoi in two places: after a preposition (à quoi, de quoi) and at the end of a sentence (tu fais quoi ?). At the front it is always que.
Qu'est-ce qui = thing + subject. The first half says what you ask about (que = thing), the last half says its role (qui = subject).

questions.q: Which form asks « Who did you see? »
choices: Qui est-ce que tu as vu ?
questions.why: Qui = person, and the final que = object: person + object. Qui est-ce qui would make the person the subject: who called?

questions.q: Complete with the right form of quel: « ___ villes as-tu visitées ? »
questions.why: Quel is an adjective and agrees with its noun: quel, quelle, quels, quelles. Villes is feminine plural.

questions.q: Why is it « Quelle est ton adresse ? » and not « Qu'est-ce que ton adresse ? »
choices: Quel is used when a noun is involved; qu'est-ce que when there is none
Qu'est-ce que cannot start a sentence
questions.why: Quel goes with a noun, even when être stands between them: quelle heure, quel âge, quel est le problème. Qu'est-ce que is for nounless questions: qu'est-ce que tu fais.
Age is masculine, so quel with no -e, and inversion with tu is normal in this set phrase.

questions.q: Say this out loud: Why is the sky blue?
questions.why: With pourquoi and a noun subject, the noun stays and a pronoun echoes it after the verb. In speech you could simply say Pourquoi le ciel est bleu ?

questions.q: Explain the four long forms: qu'est-ce qui, qu'est-ce que, qui est-ce qui, qui est-ce que. Give an example of each.
a: The first half says what you are asking about (qui = person, que = thing), the last half says its grammatical role (qui = subject, que = object). Qu'est-ce qui se passe ? (thing, subject) · Qu'est-ce que tu fais ? (thing, object) · Qui est-ce qui a téléphoné ? (person, subject) · Qui est-ce que tu as vu ? (person, object).
questions.why: Once you read them as two halves they decode themselves, which beats memorising four separate strings.
